entities.summary:
The I Ching, or Yijing, is an ancient Chinese text that dates back to the Western Zhou period (c. 1000–750 BC), making it one of the oldest classics in Chinese literature. It serves as a foundational work in the realms of divination, philosophy, and cosmology, influencing not only Chinese thought but also the global understanding of fate and decision-making. Its significance extends beyond its geographical origin, impacting various cultures across Asia and later the Western world, where it has been adopted by philosophers, artists, and scholars alike, including figures such as Carl Jung, who integrated its concepts into modern psychological thought.

Initially a divination manual, the I Ching evolved through the Warring States period and early imperial eras (c. 500–200 BC) into a complex cosmological text enriched by commentaries known as the Ten Wings. These additions provided philosophical insights on the nature of change and the universe, reflecting the dynamic interplay of yin and yang, and the concept of hexagrams that depict life’s myriad situations. The text's incorporation into the Chinese Five Classics solidified its status as a central pillar of Confucian education, ensuring its doctrines shaped governance, ethics, and personal conduct throughout Chinese history.

The legacy of the I Ching is profound; it has influenced various disciplines such as philosophy, art, and even politics across centuries. Its concepts of change and duality resonate in modern strategic thinking and decision-making frameworks, as well as in practices like Feng Shui. The text has been translated into numerous languages, reaching a global audience and inspiring interpretations that connect Eastern and Western philosophies. As the philosopher Thomas Cleary noted, 'The I Ching is not just a text; it’s a living tradition that continues to evolve.'

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The I Ching (易經, Yì Jīng, 'Classic of Changes' or 'Book of Changes') is one of the oldest and most influential texts in the world — a Chinese divination manual and philosophical classic, probably reaching its textual form during the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1000–750 BCE), though its core component, the 64 hexagrams (six-line symbols composed of broken and unbroken lines), may be significantly older. The I Ching is one of the Five Classics of Confucian literature (alongside the Book of Odes, Book of Documents, Book of Rites, and Spring and Autumn Annals) and is the foundation of traditional Chinese cosmological, philosophical, and ethical thought. It was the primary resource for the traditional Chinese practice of divination (yarrow stalk casting, coin tossing) and has been continuously used for divinatory, philosophical, and literary purposes for over three thousand years.

The I Ching's structure consists of 64 hexagrams — binary symbols formed from combinations of six yin (broken, −−) and yang (unbroken, —) lines, representing all possible combinations of change — each accompanied by a brief textual statement (the gua ci, hexagram statement) and six additional statements for each individual line (the yao ci, line statements), traditionally attributed to King Wen of Zhou (the hexagram statements) and the Duke of Zhou (the line statements). These core texts are supplemented by the Ten Wings (Shi Yi), a set of philosophical commentaries traditionally attributed to Confucius (though modern scholarship dates them to the Warring States period, 5th–3rd century BCE), which transform the divination manual into a philosophical text on the nature of change, the cosmos, and human virtue.

The I Ching's influence extends far beyond China — introduced to Europe via the Jesuit missionaries and their translations (notably Leibniz's encounter with the binary hexagrams in 1701, which influenced his development of binary arithmetic), translated by Richard Wilhelm (I Ging, 1923 — the most influential Western translation), and adopted by the Western counter-culture in the 1960s–1970s.
